Verify Now Blog > PCB Layout Design Process from Schematic to Manufacturing PCB Layout Design Process from Schematic to Manufacturing by: Mila Sep 16,2025 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Design & Layout pcb layout design schematic design pcb layout services pcb layout design services PCB layout design is the process of transforming an electrical schematic into a complete, manufacturable printed circuit board (PCB). A well-designed PCB layout must do more than simply connect components. It needs to balance electrical performance, signal integrity, power integrity, thermal management, mechanical constraints, manufacturability, and reliability. For complex electronic products, decisions made during PCB layout can have a significant impact on product performance, production yield, cost, and time to market. A professional PCB layout workflow therefore requires systematic planning, engineering review, design verification, and manufacturing preparation. Below is an overview of the PCB layout design process we follow, from the initial schematic review to final manufacturing data.You can also find more information on our PCB Layout page . Step 1 – Design Preparation and Engineering Review The PCB layout process begins with a detailed review of the design requirements and source files. Before starting the layout, our engineers review the schematic and project specifications to make sure the design is ready for PCB implementation. This includes checking: Schematic completeness and connectivity Component information and footprints Board dimensions and mechanical constraints Layer count and stack-up requirements Component placement restrictions High-speed and differential signals Power distribution requirements Impedance-control requirements Thermal considerations Manufacturing capabilities and design rules If the customer only provides a PDF or image-based schematic, we can recreate the schematic in professional EDA software before proceeding with PCB layout. If the original schematic file is available, we can directly import the design data, generate the netlist, and establish the PCB design environment. At this stage, we also identify potential design issues that could affect layout, manufacturing, or product performance. Resolving these issues early helps reduce design iterations later in the process. Step 2 – PCB Stack-Up and Design Rule Setup Before component placement and routing, the PCB layer structure and key design rules need to be established. For multilayer and high-speed PCBs, the stack-up directly affects signal integrity, impedance control, power integrity, EMI performance, and manufacturability. Depending on the application, we may define: Number of PCB layers Core and prepreg materials Copper thickness Dielectric thickness Controlled impedance requirements Power and ground reference planes Minimum trace width and spacing Via structures and drill sizes Manufacturing constraints For high-speed designs, impedance-controlled traces and their reference planes are considered from the beginning rather than being treated as an afterthought. The design rules are then configured in the EDA software to ensure that the layout remains consistent with both the electrical requirements and the PCB manufacturer's manufacturing capabilities. Step 3 – Component Placement Component placement is one of the most important stages of PCB layout because it establishes the physical structure of the entire board. The placement strategy typically starts with components whose locations are constrained by the mechanical design, such as: Connectors Switches and buttons Mounting holes Displays Mechanical interfaces Heat sinks and other thermal components Core components such as MCUs, CPUs, FPGAs, memory devices, power ICs, and communication ICs are then positioned according to signal flow, functional relationships, and electrical requirements. Supporting components are placed close to their corresponding devices to minimize unnecessary routing length and improve electrical performance. During placement, we consider several factors simultaneously: Signal Integrity High-speed interfaces and sensitive signals require appropriate component relationships and short, well-controlled routing paths. Power Integrity Decoupling capacitors should be positioned close to the relevant power pins, while power distribution paths should be kept short and low impedance. Thermal Management Heat-generating components need sufficient copper area, thermal vias, airflow consideration, and appropriate spacing from temperature-sensitive devices. EMI/EMC Performance Sensitive analog circuits, high-speed digital circuits, switching power supplies, and other potential noise sources need to be appropriately positioned to reduce interference. Manufacturability Component spacing, assembly orientation, soldering requirements, and accessibility for inspection and rework are also considered. A well-planned placement makes subsequent routing more efficient while improving the overall reliability and manufacturability of the PCB. Step 4 – PCB Routing Once the component placement is finalized, the next stage is PCB routing. Routing is not simply about finding a path between two pads. The routing strategy must consider electrical performance, signal integrity, power distribution, EMI/EMC, and manufacturing constraints. Depending on the design, routing priorities may include: High-Speed and Critical Signals High-speed interfaces such as USB, DDR, PCIe, Ethernet, HDMI, LVDS, and other differential interfaces may require: Controlled impedance Differential-pair routing Length matching Skew control Appropriate reference planes Minimized discontinuities Careful via transitions Critical signals are routed according to their electrical requirements rather than simply following the shortest available path. Power and Ground Power distribution networks are designed to provide stable and low-impedance power delivery. Ground planes are carefully maintained to provide appropriate return paths and reduce unwanted noise and electromagnetic interference. General Signals After critical nets have been addressed, general signal routing is completed according to the defined design rules for: Trace width Trace spacing Via size Clearance Routing layers Manufacturing limitations For dense boards, routing may require multiple iterations of placement and routing optimization to achieve a balance between electrical performance and manufacturability. Step 5– Layout Optimization and Verification After routing is completed, the PCB layout undergoes a detailed optimization and verification process. This stage may include: Copper Pour and Plane Optimization Copper pours and power/ground planes are optimized to improve current return paths, grounding, shielding, and thermal performance. Silkscreen Optimization Reference designators, polarity markings, pin-1 indicators, and other assembly information are adjusted to improve readability and prevent interference with pads or other components. Design Rule Check (DRC) Automated DRC is performed to identify potential violations such as: Clearance violations Trace width violations Unconnected nets Via and drill violations Component spacing issues Copper-to-board-edge violations Other manufacturer-specific rule violations Engineer Review Beyond automated DRC, the layout is also reviewed from an engineering perspective. Depending on the project, this may include checking: Signal integrity Power integrity Thermal performance EMI/EMC considerations High-speed routing Manufacturing constraints Assembly requirements Mechanical compatibility Automated checks can identify rule violations, but they cannot replace engineering judgment. A professional PCB review therefore combines software-based verification with engineering inspection. Step 6 – Design Review and Customer Approval Before generating final manufacturing data, the completed PCB layout is provided to the customer for review. The customer can verify key aspects of the design, including: Component locations Board dimensions Connector positions Mechanical interfaces Silkscreen information Routing and design intent Any required changes are incorporated before the design is released for manufacturing. This review stage provides an important checkpoint between PCB design and production and helps ensure that the final layout accurately reflects the customer's design requirements. Step 7 – Manufacturing Data Generation Once the PCB layout has been approved, the final manufacturing data is generated. Depending on the project, the manufacturing package may include: Gerber files NC drill files PCB fabrication drawings Bill of Materials (BOM) Pick-and-place files Assembly drawings Stack-up information Other manufacturing documentation Gerber files contain the graphical information required to manufacture the PCB, including copper layers, solder mask, silkscreen, and other fabrication layers. For PCB assembly projects, the BOM and pick-and-place files provide the component and placement information required for SMT assembly. Before release, the output files are checked to ensure that the generated manufacturing data is consistent with the approved PCB design. Step 8 – DFM and PCB Manufacturing The final stage is transferring the verified manufacturing data into production. Before fabrication, the manufacturing data can be evaluated against the PCB manufacturer's capabilities through Design for Manufacturability (DFM) checks. Typical DFM considerations include: Minimum trace width and spacing Minimum drill size Copper-to-edge clearance Annular ring requirements Solder mask clearance Via structures Board thickness Copper thickness Surface finish Manufacturing tolerances Manufacturing requirements are considered from the very beginning of PCBWay's PCB layout process, helping minimize production issues and unnecessary manufacturing delays. What’s more, upon completion of the PCB Layout order, free technical support and a permanent 5% discount on PCBA production will be provided. Why Professional PCB Layout Matters PCB layout has a direct impact on the performance and manufacturability of an electronic product. A professional PCB layout should consider the entire product development process—not just whether all components are electrically connected. Depending on the application, the layout may need to address: Signal Integrity (SI) Power Integrity (PI) EMI/EMC Thermal Management High-Speed Design Design for Manufacturability (DFM) Design for Assembly (DFA) Mechanical Integration Reliability and Serviceability The earlier these factors are considered, the fewer problems are likely to appear during prototype validation and mass production. At PCBWay, our PCB design engineers work with customers throughout the layout process, helping transform circuit concepts and schematics into manufacturable, reliable, and production-ready PCB designs. If you are looking for professional PCB layout or PCB design services, feel free to contact us or submit PCB Layout requirement here. Our engineering team can help evaluate your design and develop a PCB layout optimized for both performance and manufacturing. Verify Now Blog > Power Supply Design and Layout Guidelines for LDO and DCDC Power Supply Design and Layout Guidelines for LDO and DCDC by: Mila Sep 29,2026 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Design & Layout power supply design DCDC PCB layout power supply layout LDO layout guidelines Power supply design is not simply about choosing the right regulator and adding enough copper. The PCB layout directly affects thermal performance, noise, EMI, stability, and overall power integrity. LDOs and DCDC converters have different layout priorities: LDOs require careful attention to heat dissipation, capacitor placement, and power loss, while DCDC converters are more sensitive to high-frequency current loops, feedback routing, and grounding. When both are used in the same system, power-stage isolation and decoupling become equally important. In this guide, we’ll break down the key power supply layout considerations and common mistakes for LDOs, DCDC converters, and mixed power architectures. 1. LDO (Low-Dropout Regulator): Quiet but Sensitive to Heat （LDO regulator） Advantages: Low noise, no switching interference, and simple peripheral circuitry Disadvantages: Efficiency depends on the input-to-output voltage difference, and large voltage drops or high load currents can generate significant heat. Three Common LDO PCB Layout Mistakes Mistake 1: Poor Thermal Management → Excessive Temperature Rise Incorrect: Leaving the exposed pad floating without sufficient copper area or thermal vias. Consequence: Higher thermal resistance can increase junction temperature, potentially triggering thermal protection or affecting long-term reliability. Correct: Connect the exposed pad to a sufficiently large copper area. Add thermal vias according to the package and datasheet recommendations, connecting them to internal or bottom-layer copper planes. Avoid routing signal traces underneath the thermal pad. Evaluate the required copper area and thermal performance based on actual power dissipation. Mistake 2: Input/Output Capacitors Too Far from the Pins → Reduced Stability and Transient Performance Incorrect: Placing the input and output capacitors far away from the LDO pins. Consequence: Increased parasitic impedance can affect stability, transient response, and high-frequency noise performance. Correct: Place Cin and Cout as close as possible to the corresponding LDO pins. Select capacitor values, quantities, and ESR according to the device datasheet. Prefer low-ESR capacitors recommended by the manufacturer. Keep the feedback path short and avoid unnecessary routing and noise coupling. Mistake 3: Ignoring Voltage Drop and Power Dissipation → Efficiency and Thermal Issues Incorrect: Using an LDO for high input voltage and high current without evaluating power dissipation. Consequence: Higher LDO power dissipation increases junction temperature and may trigger thermal protection or reduce system reliability. Correct: The main power dissipation of an LDO can be estimated using: P ≈ (Vin − Vout) × Iout The larger the voltage drop and output current, the higher the LDO power dissipation. For high-power applications, evaluate efficiency, junction temperature, and PCB thermal performance together. When the voltage drop or load current is high, consider using a DCDC converter first and an LDO for downstream regulation and noise reduction. 2. DCDC (Switching Power Supply): Efficient but Noisy （dc-dc converter） Advantages: High conversion efficiency, higher output current capability, and suitability for a wide range of input and output voltages Disadvantages: Switching nodes and high di/dt currents can generate noise, making DCDC PCB layout critical to EMI, stability, and overall power performance. Five Common DCDC PCB Layout Mistakes Mistake 1: Long Power Loops → Increased Ringing and EMI Incorrect: Placing the input capacitor, power switch, inductor, and other key components too far apart, resulting in a large high-frequency current loop. Consequence: Increased parasitic inductance can produce more pronounced voltage spikes and ringing under high di/dt conditions, increasing EMI and component stress. Correct: Minimize the area of critical high-frequency power loops. Place input bypass capacitors, power devices, and inductors as close together as possible. Use sufficiently wide power traces. The required width should be determined by current, copper thickness, and allowable temperature rise. Avoid unnecessarily long high di/dt return paths. Mistake 2: Noisy Feedback Path → Output Voltage Fluctuation Incorrect: Routing the FB trace close to or parallel with the SW node, inductor, or other noisy areas. Consequence: Switching noise can couple into the feedback network, affecting output voltage regulation and system stability. Correct: Keep the FB trace short and away from the SW node and high di/dt current paths. Place the feedback resistors close to the IC's FB pin. Sense the output voltage from a stable, low-noise point. For high-precision applications, consider Kelvin sensing or other methods recommended by the device manufacturer to reduce voltage drop and noise. Mistake 3: Improper Ground Plane Design → Increased EMI and Noise Incorrect: Improper AGND, PGND, or high-current return-path routing causes sensitive control circuitry to share impedance with power return currents. Consequence: Ground bounce and common-impedance coupling can affect control signals, feedback, and output voltage. Correct: Follow the DCDC IC manufacturer's recommended method for connecting AGND and PGND. Provide a low-impedance return path for PGND. Keep sensitive analog ground areas away from high-current power return paths whenever possible. Prevent high di/dt currents from passing through sensitive signal areas. Mistake 4: Improper Input Capacitor Placement → Increased Input Ripple Incorrect: Relying on a single bulk capacitor while placing it far from the VIN and GND pins. Consequence: A larger high-frequency current loop can increase input ripple and noise. Correct: Configure input capacitors according to the DCDC converter datasheet. Use capacitors with different values when necessary to address different frequency ranges. Place input capacitors as close as possible to the VIN and GND pins. Keep the input capacitor loop short and compact. Mistake 5: Ignoring the Freewheeling Path → Reduced Efficiency and Poorer EMI Performance Incorrect: Placing the freewheeling diode, synchronous MOSFET, or related circuitry too far apart. Consequence: Increased parasitic parameters can lead to additional losses, ringing, and EMI. Correct: Optimize the freewheeling and synchronous rectification paths according to the specific converter topology. Minimize high-current return paths. For multiphase DCDC converters, keep the power paths of each phase well organized and reasonably symmetrical. 3. LDO + DCDC Mixed Power Supply: Balancing Efficiency and Low Noise （power supply pcb） In practical systems, DCDC converters and LDOs are often used together rather than as alternatives. For example: DCDC: 12V → 3.3V for efficient voltage conversion LDO: 3.3V → 1.8V for noise-sensitive circuits such as ADCs, PLLs, and clocks This approach combines the efficiency of a DCDC converter with the low-noise characteristics of an LDO, making it useful for applications that require both power efficiency and clean power rails. Three Common Mixed Power Supply Layout Mistakes Mistake 1: Insufficient Filtering at the LDO Input → Upstream Noise May Reach the Downstream Rail Incorrect: Connecting the DCDC output directly to an LDO-powered sensitive load without evaluating the DCDC switching noise and the LDO's PSRR. Consequence: Switching ripple from the upstream converter may couple into downstream sensitive circuits through the power path, affecting ADC, PLL, and other noise-sensitive devices. Correct: Evaluate whether additional filtering is required based on the DCDC switching frequency, LDO PSRR, and load noise requirements. When necessary, add a ferrite bead, LC filter, or π filter between the two power stages. Place filtering components close to the corresponding power input and keep the filter loop area under control. Avoid adding filtering components blindly; select them based on the actual noise frequency range. Mistake 2: Poor Power Region Layout → Noise Coupling Incorrect: Placing the high-noise DCDC switching area too close to sensitive LDO power areas or creating unnecessary coupling between different power regions. Consequence: Switching noise can couple into sensitive power rails through parasitic capacitance, electromagnetic coupling, or shared impedance. Correct: Properly separate the DCDC power stage, LDO area, and sensitive load areas. Keep high-noise SW nodes away from sensitive power rails and signals. Maintain a solid reference ground plane beneath the LDO output power area whenever possible. Keep sensitive power traces away from high di/dt return paths of the DCDC converter. Mistake 3: Poorly Designed Decoupling Network → Insufficient High-Frequency Response Incorrect: Placing all capacitors at the DCDC output while providing insufficient local decoupling near sensitive loads. Consequence: Parasitic impedance in the power path can reduce high-frequency decoupling effectiveness, preventing the load from receiving transient current quickly enough. Correct: Configure DCDC output capacitors according to the converter requirements. Use the required input and output capacitors at the LDO according to the datasheet. Add local decoupling capacitors close to sensitive loads such as ADCs, PLLs, and MCUs. Design each power stage's decoupling network according to the actual load and frequency requirements rather than simply adding more capacitors. Conclusion Although LDOs and DCDC converters are both power management devices, their power supply layout priorities are different. LDO layout guidelines focus more on thermal management, capacitor placement, and power dissipation. DCDC PCB layout focuses more on high-frequency power loops, feedback paths, grounding, and EMI. Mixed power supplies require additional attention to noise isolation and decoupling between different power stages. A good power supply pcb design is not simply about adding more copper. It is about giving current the shortest and most appropriate path, keeping noise away from sensitive areas, and placing every critical component where it can perform properly. Verify Now Blog > Why Antipads Matter for Signal Integrity in High-Speed PCB Design Why Antipads Matter for Signal Integrity in High-Speed PCB Design by: Mila Sep 21,2026 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Design & Layout signal integrity PCB antipad high-speed PCB design anti pad pcb In high-speed PCB design , via antipads are often treated as simple clearance features. In fact, the size of a PCB antipad directly affects the parasitic capacitance and local impedance around a via, making it an important parameter for maintaining impedance continuity and signal integrity. If the antipad is too small, it can introduce excessive capacitive loading and cause local impedance to drop. If it is too large, it may affect the integrity of the power or ground plane. Especially in Gbps-level high-speed links, simply using the default parameters in PCB design software can result in significant impedance discontinuities around the via transition, potentially affecting signal integrity. The purpose of an anti pad PCB design is not limited to preventing electrical shorts. By changing the electromagnetic coupling between the via and reference plane, a properly designed antipad can reduce via parasitic capacitance, optimize local impedance, and minimize signal reflections. Therefore, antipad design is an important part of optimizing high-speed vias. What Is a PCB Antipad Actually “Removing”? Let's put aside the abstract definition and look at it from a straightforward engineering perspective. When a PCB via changes layers, its metal barrel and pad pass through portions of the power and ground planes. The metal conductor, dielectric material, and surrounding plane copper naturally form parasitic capacitance. The impedance of a transmission line is mainly determined by the dielectric material, trace width, and stackup. However, the additional parasitic capacitance around a via introduces extra capacitive loading, causing the local via impedance to deviate from the target impedance of the transmission line. This creates an impedance discontinuity that can affect high-speed signal transmission. A PCB antipad is a copper clearance area created around the via pad on the power or ground plane layers through which the via passes. Its main purposes are: Increase the distance between the via barrel and plane copper to prevent electrical shorts; Reduce the parasitic capacitance between the via and reference plane, optimize local via impedance, and reduce reflections caused by impedance discontinuity. A high-speed signal trace can be compared to a smooth road with a constant speed limit. The via is an unavoidable intersection, while parasitic capacitance is like a sudden dip in the road. When the signal travels through this discontinuity at high speed, impedance changes can cause reflections, ringing, and waveform distortion. The purpose of an antipad is to adjust the electromagnetic coupling between the via and reference plane, reducing the impact of this “dip” and making the via transition smoother. （Anti-pad Structure） How Does Parasitic Capacitance Affect Via Impedance? A via is not an ideal conductor. Its equivalent model can include parasitic inductance L and parasitic capacitance C. For high-speed signals, the actual impedance characteristics of a via are also affected by factors such as via length, hole diameter, pad size, antipad size, reference plane position, and via stub. The antipad size is one of the important parameters affecting via parasitic capacitance. If the antipad is too small, the distance between the via barrel or pad and the reference plane becomes smaller, increasing the capacitive loading between the via and plane. This can cause a more significant drop in local via impedance. For example, when a transmission line with a target impedance of 50 Ω passes through an unoptimized via structure, the local impedance may decrease around the via transition, creating a structure such as: 50 Ω trace → lower impedance at via → 50 Ω trace. This impedance discontinuity can cause signal reflections, energy loss, and waveform distortion. Therefore, an antipad is not simply a matter of making the clearance as large or as small as possible. In high-speed PCB design, its size needs to be optimized together with the stackup, via structure, and target impedance. （Small antipad vs Large antipad） What Problems Can Improper Antipad Design Cause? It is easy to assume that a small dimensional difference will not matter. However, in Gbps-level high-speed links, even small geometric changes in the via structure can affect impedance and signal integrity. 1. Impedance Discontinuity, Signal Reflection, and Reduced Eye Opening A smaller antipad → higher parasitic capacitance → potentially lower local via impedance. When a high-speed signal reaches this region, a significant impedance change can cause signal reflection, edge distortion, increased jitter, and reduced eye opening. These effects may ultimately degrade the performance of the high-speed link. 2. Poorer Return Loss and Reflected Signal Energy Impedance discontinuities increase signal reflection, causing part of the signal energy to return toward the transmitter instead of reaching the receiver effectively. For high-speed SerDes links, reflections from multiple vias, connectors, and package structures can accumulate. Therefore, maintaining impedance continuity across the via transition is an important part of signal integrity optimization. 3. Via Resonance and Stub Effects Can Increase Loss at Specific Frequencies The parasitic inductance and capacitance of a via, together with unused via stubs, can create frequency-dependent resonance and reflection characteristics. When the effective frequency range of a high-speed signal approaches these resonant regions, return loss and insertion loss may deteriorate significantly. This is one reason why some links may work normally at lower speeds but show degraded performance at higher data rates. Therefore, in addition to PCB antipad design, high-speed via design also needs to consider via stubs. For loss-sensitive high-speed links, techniques such as back drilling, blind vias, or buried vias can be used to shorten or eliminate unnecessary via stubs. 4. Reference Plane Discontinuity and Poorer Return Current Paths An antipad should not simply be made as large as possible. If the plane clearance becomes excessively large, it may affect the continuity of the local reference plane and force the high-speed return current to take a longer path. This can increase return-path inductance and introduce additional impedance discontinuities. In high-density high-speed PCB design, the locations of adjacent vias, return vias, and reference planes should also be considered together to avoid creating new signal integrity or EMI problems through excessive plane clearance. Not Just Vias: BGA Areas Also Need Attention Most high-speed PCB designs focus heavily on via antipads, but in high-density BGA regions, the parasitic capacitance between component pads and reference planes also deserves attention. A typical high-speed trace may be only 3–4 mil wide, while a BGA pad is usually much larger than the trace. The larger the pad area and the closer it is to the reference plane, the greater the potential capacitive loading. A large pad located close to a reference plane can introduce additional capacitive loading, making the BGA breakout region another potential impedance transition in a high-speed signal path. Therefore, high-speed BGA design should consider: BGA pad size; Distance between the pad and reference plane; Trace width and impedance; Breakout method; Reference plane continuity. When necessary, local plane clearance can be used to reduce the parasitic capacitance associated with the pad. However, not every BGA pad requires an enlarged antipad. Excessive plane clearance can also disrupt reference plane continuity and force the return current to detour. Therefore, the appropriate clearance should be determined based on the stackup, pad geometry, target impedance, and simulation results. How Should a Differential Via Antipad Be Designed? A single-ended signal via can typically use a circular antipad, but differential vias should not simply follow the same design approach. 1. Separate Circular Antipads May Introduce Additional Coupling If the positive and negative differential vias each use an independent circular antipad, a narrow strip of reference plane copper may remain between the two antipads. This remaining copper can change the electromagnetic coupling between the two vias. For high-speed differential signals, such a structural change may affect: Differential impedance Symmetry between the two signal paths Differential-to-common-mode conversion Insertion loss and return loss around the via transition 2. This approach can reduce unnecessary plane copper between the two vias and create a more symmetrical electromagnetic environment around the differential via pair. The main benefits include: Better control of differential impedance toward the target value; Improved structural symmetry and reduced risk of differential-to-common-mode conversion; Reduced unnecessary local electromagnetic coupling between the vias. However, a dog-bone-shaped antipad is not a universal solution for every differential via structure. The final shape and dimensions should still be determined based on via spacing, stackup, target impedance, and simulation results. How Large Should a PCB Antipad Be? Antipad design is a typical case of “too much of a good thing.” If the antipad is too small, electromagnetic coupling between the via and reference plane increases, potentially increasing parasitic capacitance. If it is too large, reference plane continuity may be affected. Therefore, the PCB antipad needs to balance impedance control, return current paths, and manufacturing capability. Key Guidelines for High-Speed PCB Antipad Design 1. Do Not Simply Apply a Fixed Mil Value There is no universal antipad size that works for every high-speed PCB. The actual dimensions should be optimized according to via hole diameter, pad size, dielectric thickness, material Dk, reference plane position, and target impedance. 2. Meet Manufacturing Rules Before Optimizing Impedance An initial antipad size can be established according to the PCB manufacturer's design rules and then refined through impedance calculation or simulation. 3. Maintain Symmetry in Differential Vias For differential via structures, the geometry and electromagnetic environment around the positive and negative vias should be as symmetrical as possible to maintain differential impedance and reduce mode conversion. 4. Simulate the Complete Via Transition for High-Speed Links For high-speed links above 10 Gbps, as well as interfaces such as PCIe, USB, and SerDes that have strict requirements for channel loss and impedance continuity, fixed empirical dimensions should not be applied directly. The complete stackup, material Dk/Df, via geometry, reference planes, return vias, and target impedance should be considered together. For complex three-dimensional via structures, tools such as HFSS, CST, or Simbeor can be used for electromagnetic analysis, while tools such as Polar SI9000 are more suitable for PCB stackup and transmission-line impedance analysis. The acceptable impedance variation should ultimately be determined according to the specific interface specification and channel budget rather than applying a single universal ±10% requirement. Conclusion Effective high-speed PCB design is not simply about creating an antipad around a via. It requires an understanding of the relationship between parasitic capacitance, via impedance, reference planes, return current paths, and signal integrity. An antipad that is too small may increase capacitive loading and cause local impedance to decrease, while an oversized antipad may affect reference plane continuity. For high-speed differential vias, designers must also consider structural symmetry, differential impedance, and mode conversion. Therefore, there is no single antipad size that is suitable for every PCB. A properly designed PCB antipad should be optimized according to the target impedance and signal integrity requirements, together with the PCB stackup, via geometry, manufacturing capability, and simulation results. This helps maintain a more continuous and stable electromagnetic environment throughout the high-speed signal path. Enter the year of your birth and check your Chinese Zodiac. Why Do PCBs Need Stitching Vias Along the Board Edge? by: Mila Oct 07,2026 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Design & Layout stitching vias PCB EMI shielding PCB return path PCB via stitching Anyone who has worked on PCB layout has probably experienced this: after finishing the layout, you hand the board over to a senior engineer for review. They take a quick look around the board and ask, “Where are the ground vias along the edge?” At first, this may seem unnecessary. After all, the board edge does not carry signal traces. So why are stitching vias placed there? The answer lies in what happens around the edge of a PCB. Properly placed grounding vias can help control electromagnetic coupling, provide a more continuous high-frequency return path, and improve PCB edge shielding. For high-speed, RF, and EMI-sensitive designs, that simple row of vias can make a noticeable difference. （Stitching Vias） What Do Ground Vias Along the PCB Edge Actually Do? This row of vias is commonly known as a ground via fence, via fence, or stitching vias. It is not simply a matter of placing a row of vias around the board. Instead, the vias connect ground structures on different PCB layers and create a more continuous electromagnetic boundary along the board edge. For high-speed, RF, and high-reliability PCBs, the main benefits include improving high-frequency return paths, reducing electromagnetic leakage and coupling, and enhancing the continuity of local shielding structures. 1. Reduce Electromagnetic Leakage and Improve EMI Performance The PCB edge is the boundary between copper, dielectric material, and air. When high-speed, clock, or RF signals pass through the board, relatively strong electromagnetic fields may exist around this region. If the reference ground structure around the PCB edge is discontinuous, electromagnetic fields can couple outward through the edge, increasing EMI risks. External interference can also couple into sensitive circuits through the same region. A continuous row of grounding vias creates a low-impedance grounding boundary around the PCB edge. It can help limit the spread of electromagnetic fields around the edge and reduce coupling between the signals and the surrounding environment, improving EMI performance. 2. Provide a More Continuous High-Frequency Return Path High-speed signal return current generally follows a path close to the signal trace and its reference plane. When a PCB contains multiple ground or reference planes, insufficient connections between these planes can force high-frequency return currents to take longer paths, increasing both return path length and loop area. Stitching vias can provide low-impedance connections between different ground layers, giving high-frequency currents a more continuous return path. The more continuous the return path, the smaller the loop area can be, making electromagnetic radiation and crosstalk easier to control. 3. Help Reduce Edge Coupling and Local Resonance For RF, microwave, and high-speed clock PCBs, discontinuities around the board edge can create additional electromagnetic coupling paths and, at certain frequencies, may contribute to unwanted resonance. A continuous row of grounding vias can improve the electromagnetic boundary conditions around the PCB edge, reduce edge coupling, and help suppress local resonance. This is particularly useful in RF regions, shielding areas, and areas with dense high-speed signals, where a properly designed PCB ground via fence can be more effective than simply adding more copper. 4. Provide a Continuous Grounding Point for Shielding Cans RF modules and high-speed precision modules often use metal shielding cans. In this case, grounding vias can work together with the shielding-can solder pad to create a more continuous low-impedance grounding path around the shield. If a shielding can has only a few grounding points, the parasitic inductance of the connection path can affect high-frequency shielding performance. Adding stitching vias around the shielding-can edge can shorten the high-frequency current path and reduce electromagnetic leakage around the shield. Therefore, a via fence around a shielding can is generally more suitable for high-frequency shielding than a single-point ground connection. （EMI shielding + stitching vias） Faraday Cage: Why Can a Row of Ground Vias Help With Shielding? Many engineers think of the grounding vias around a PCB edge as a small Faraday cage. There is some truth to this analogy, but an important point should be noted: a PCB via fence is not an ideal, completely enclosed Faraday cage. The basic idea behind a Faraday cage is to use a continuous conductive structure to shield against electromagnetic fields through reflection, absorption, and boundary effects. On a PCB, continuous ground copper, reference planes, stitching vias, and metal shielding cans can work together to create a similar shielding structure. One important function of the grounding vias is to connect ground structures on different layers and reduce electromagnetic “openings” around the PCB edge. At high frequencies, shielding effectiveness depends on many factors, including conductor continuity, via spacing, opening size, material, operating frequency, and the overall structure. Therefore, instead of simply applying a fixed wavelength ratio, the via spacing should be determined based on the actual operating frequency, signal rise time, and PCB structure. For high-speed digital signals, the relevant frequency content is not necessarily equal to the clock frequency. Signal rise time also needs to be considered. Limitations A PCB via fence cannot completely prevent electromagnetic coupling at all frequencies. Copper and grounding vias alone have limited effectiveness against low-frequency magnetic fields. At high frequencies, the parasitic inductance, spacing, and structure of the vias can affect shielding performance. The effectiveness of the shielding structure also depends on the PCB reference planes, return paths, connectors, shielding cans, and other design elements. How Should You Design Stitching Vias Along the PCB Edge? Adding vias around the board is not simply a matter of placing them in a row. Via spacing, location, grounding method, and edge copper design all need to be considered according to the actual PCB structure. Here are some common design principles. 1. Via Spacing A common engineering approach is to estimate the via spacing based on the wavelength corresponding to the target frequency. For example, λ/10 or a smaller spacing can be used as an initial reference. However, this is not a fixed standard that applies to every PCB. Actual design should also consider: The highest frequency of interest High-speed signal rise/fall time PCB stackup Reference plane location Board-edge structure Shielding-can and connector openings For ordinary PCBs, relatively wider via spacing may be sufficient. For high-speed, RF, or high-EMI areas, the spacing may need to be reduced. Common engineering reference values include: General PCBs: approximately 50–100 mil High-speed/RF areas: approximately 30–50 mil Areas with stringent shielding requirements: further spacing reduction based on simulation or actual EMI testing Do not mechanically apply a fixed value. The final via spacing should be determined based on the actual frequency and structure. 2. Via Location Edge grounding vias should maintain an appropriate clearance from the PCB outline. Sufficient clearance should be provided according to the PCB manufacturer's fabrication capability to prevent damage to the vias during routing, milling, V-cut, or other board-edge processing. At the same time: Distribute the vias evenly along the board edge whenever possible. Avoid large gaps in the via fence. Increase via density around RF, high-speed signal, and connector areas when necessary. Connect the grounding vias to the appropriate reference ground plane rather than only to the top-layer copper. It is important to note that not every ground plane needs to be connected through the same via. The exact connection method should be determined based on the PCB stackup and return-current path. 3. Start With Continuous Ground Copper Many designers add a row of vias but overlook the ground copper between them. This alone cannot create a complete PCB ground via fence. A continuous ground copper area should be provided around the PCB edge according to the board structure, with grounding vias connecting it to the internal reference ground plane. The vias provide vertical connections, while continuous ground copper provides horizontal connections. Together, they form a more complete grounding boundary. High-speed signal traces, slots, or other structures should not arbitrarily cut through this grounding boundary. 4. Increase Via Density in Critical Areas The entire PCB does not necessarily need the same via spacing. The following areas may require additional stitching vias: Board-edge connectors and interfaces: Connectors are important paths through which external signals enter the PCB. Proper grounding vias can improve the return path around the interface and reduce edge coupling. Shielding-can areas: Dense grounding vias around the shielding-can solder pad can create a more continuous high-frequency grounding path. RF and high-speed clock areas: For areas that are particularly sensitive to EMI or crosstalk, reducing the via spacing can strengthen local shielding. Conclusion Proper stitching vias are an important part of high-speed PCB layout and PCB design .Their core function is to improve high-frequency return paths around the PCB edge and reduce electromagnetic coupling and EMI leakage through the combination of stitching vias and continuous reference-ground structures. For high-speed, RF, and EMI-sensitive PCBs, proper PCB via stitching and PCB edge shielding are particularly important. But remember: more vias are not always better, and not every PCB needs a dense row of grounding vias. Via spacing, edge clearance, reference planes, and local shielding structures should all be determined based on the actual signal frequency, rise time, and PCB stackup. Why Do PCBs Need Stitching Vias Along the Board Edge? by: Mila Oct 07,2026 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Design & Layout stitching vias PCB EMI shielding PCB return path PCB via stitching Anyone who has worked on PCB layout has probably experienced this: after finishing the layout, you hand the board over to a senior engineer for review. They take a quick look around the board and ask, “Where are the ground vias along the edge?” At first, this may seem unnecessary. After all, the board edge does not carry signal traces. So why are stitching vias placed there? The answer lies in what happens around the edge of a PCB. Properly placed grounding vias can help control electromagnetic coupling, provide a more continuous high-frequency return path, and improve PCB edge shielding. For high-speed, RF, and EMI-sensitive designs, that simple row of vias can make a noticeable difference. （Stitching Vias） What Do Ground Vias Along the PCB Edge Actually Do? This row of vias is commonly known as a ground via fence, via fence, or stitching vias. It is not simply a matter of placing a row of vias around the board. Instead, the vias connect ground structures on different PCB layers and create a more continuous electromagnetic boundary along the board edge. For high-speed, RF, and high-reliability PCBs, the main benefits include improving high-frequency return paths, reducing electromagnetic leakage and coupling, and enhancing the continuity of local shielding structures. 1. Reduce Electromagnetic Leakage and Improve EMI Performance The PCB edge is the boundary between copper, dielectric material, and air. When high-speed, clock, or RF signals pass through the board, relatively strong electromagnetic fields may exist around this region. If the reference ground structure around the PCB edge is discontinuous, electromagnetic fields can couple outward through the edge, increasing EMI risks. External interference can also couple into sensitive circuits through the same region. A continuous row of grounding vias creates a low-impedance grounding boundary around the PCB edge. It can help limit the spread of electromagnetic fields around the edge and reduce coupling between the signals and the surrounding environment, improving EMI performance. 2. Provide a More Continuous High-Frequency Return Path High-speed signal return current generally follows a path close to the signal trace and its reference plane. When a PCB contains multiple ground or reference planes, insufficient connections between these planes can force high-frequency return currents to take longer paths, increasing both return path length and loop area. Stitching vias can provide low-impedance connections between different ground layers, giving high-frequency currents a more continuous return path. The more continuous the return path, the smaller the loop area can be, making electromagnetic radiation and crosstalk easier to control. 3. Help Reduce Edge Coupling and Local Resonance For RF, microwave, and high-speed clock PCBs, discontinuities around the board edge can create additional electromagnetic coupling paths and, at certain frequencies, may contribute to unwanted resonance. A continuous row of grounding vias can improve the electromagnetic boundary conditions around the PCB edge, reduce edge coupling, and help suppress local resonance. This is particularly useful in RF regions, shielding areas, and areas with dense high-speed signals, where a properly designed PCB ground via fence can be more effective than simply adding more copper. 4. Provide a Continuous Grounding Point for Shielding Cans RF modules and high-speed precision modules often use metal shielding cans. In this case, grounding vias can work together with the shielding-can solder pad to create a more continuous low-impedance grounding path around the shield. If a shielding can has only a few grounding points, the parasitic inductance of the connection path can affect high-frequency shielding performance. Adding stitching vias around the shielding-can edge can shorten the high-frequency current path and reduce electromagnetic leakage around the shield. Therefore, a via fence around a shielding can is generally more suitable for high-frequency shielding than a single-point ground connection. （EMI shielding + stitching vias） Faraday Cage: Why Can a Row of Ground Vias Help With Shielding? Many engineers think of the grounding vias around a PCB edge as a small Faraday cage. There is some truth to this analogy, but an important point should be noted: a PCB via fence is not an ideal, completely enclosed Faraday cage. The basic idea behind a Faraday cage is to use a continuous conductive structure to shield against electromagnetic fields through reflection, absorption, and boundary effects. On a PCB, continuous ground copper, reference planes, stitching vias, and metal shielding cans can work together to create a similar shielding structure. One important function of the grounding vias is to connect ground structures on different layers and reduce electromagnetic “openings” around the PCB edge. At high frequencies, shielding effectiveness depends on many factors, including conductor continuity, via spacing, opening size, material, operating frequency, and the overall structure. Therefore, instead of simply applying a fixed wavelength ratio, the via spacing should be determined based on the actual operating frequency, signal rise time, and PCB structure. For high-speed digital signals, the relevant frequency content is not necessarily equal to the clock frequency. Signal rise time also needs to be considered. Limitations A PCB via fence cannot completely prevent electromagnetic coupling at all frequencies. Copper and grounding vias alone have limited effectiveness against low-frequency magnetic fields. At high frequencies, the parasitic inductance, spacing, and structure of the vias can affect shielding performance. The effectiveness of the shielding structure also depends on the PCB reference planes, return paths, connectors, shielding cans, and other design elements. How Should You Design Stitching Vias Along the PCB Edge? Adding vias around the board is not simply a matter of placing them in a row. Via spacing, location, grounding method, and edge copper design all need to be considered according to the actual PCB structure. Here are some common design principles. 1. Via Spacing A common engineering approach is to estimate the via spacing based on the wavelength corresponding to the target frequency. For example, λ/10 or a smaller spacing can be used as an initial reference. However, this is not a fixed standard that applies to every PCB. Actual design should also consider: The highest frequency of interest High-speed signal rise/fall time PCB stackup Reference plane location Board-edge structure Shielding-can and connector openings For ordinary PCBs, relatively wider via spacing may be sufficient. For high-speed, RF, or high-EMI areas, the spacing may need to be reduced. Common engineering reference values include: General PCBs: approximately 50–100 mil High-speed/RF areas: approximately 30–50 mil Areas with stringent shielding requirements: further spacing reduction based on simulation or actual EMI testing Do not mechanically apply a fixed value. The final via spacing should be determined based on the actual frequency and structure. 2. Via Location Edge grounding vias should maintain an appropriate clearance from the PCB outline. Sufficient clearance should be provided according to the PCB manufacturer's fabrication capability to prevent damage to the vias during routing, milling, V-cut, or other board-edge processing. At the same time: Distribute the vias evenly along the board edge whenever possible. Avoid large gaps in the via fence. Increase via density around RF, high-speed signal, and connector areas when necessary. Connect the grounding vias to the appropriate reference ground plane rather than only to the top-layer copper. It is important to note that not every ground plane needs to be connected through the same via. The exact connection method should be determined based on the PCB stackup and return-current path. 3. Start With Continuous Ground Copper Many designers add a row of vias but overlook the ground copper between them. This alone cannot create a complete PCB ground via fence. A continuous ground copper area should be provided around the PCB edge according to the board structure, with grounding vias connecting it to the internal reference ground plane. The vias provide vertical connections, while continuous ground copper provides horizontal connections. Together, they form a more complete grounding boundary. High-speed signal traces, slots, or other structures should not arbitrarily cut through this grounding boundary. 4. Increase Via Density in Critical Areas The entire PCB does not necessarily need the same via spacing. The following areas may require additional stitching vias: Board-edge connectors and interfaces: Connectors are important paths through which external signals enter the PCB. Proper grounding vias can improve the return path around the interface and reduce edge coupling. Shielding-can areas: Dense grounding vias around the shielding-can solder pad can create a more continuous high-frequency grounding path. RF and high-speed clock areas: For areas that are particularly sensitive to EMI or crosstalk, reducing the via spacing can strengthen local shielding. Conclusion Proper stitching vias are an important part of high-speed PCB layout and PCB design .Their core function is to improve high-frequency return paths around the PCB edge and reduce electromagnetic coupling and EMI leakage through the combination of stitching vias and continuous reference-ground structures. For high-speed, RF, and EMI-sensitive PCBs, proper PCB via stitching and PCB edge shielding are particularly important. But remember: more vias are not always better, and not every PCB needs a dense row of grounding vias. Via spacing, edge clearance, reference planes, and local shielding structures should all be determined based on the actual signal frequency, rise time, and PCB stackup. Why No Traces Under a Crystal Oscillator in PCB Layout? by: Mila Sep 28,2026 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Design & Layout pcb routing crystal oscillator pcb layout pcb crystal oscillator When designing a PCB, many engineers have heard the rule: no traces should run under a crystal oscillator. But why? Can a low-speed signal trace really affect a crystal oscillator? And can a guard ring with grounding vias completely eliminate interference? Although a crystal oscillator provides the clock signal for digital circuits, its oscillation loop is highly sensitive to parasitic capacitance and external noise. Poor crystal oscillator PCB layout and PCB routing can cause frequency shifts, startup problems, or unstable clock signals, and may even increase EMI risks. So, why should traces be kept away from the area beneath a crystal? How should the guard ring and grounding vias be designed? Let's start with how a crystal oscillator works and then look at the key considerations for its PCB layout and routing. 1. How Does a Crystal Oscillator Work? A crystal oscillator uses the piezoelectric properties of a quartz crystal to generate a stable periodic signal. When an alternating voltage is applied to the crystal, it mechanically vibrates at a specific resonant frequency. The electrical and mechanical characteristics of the crystal allow it to provide a highly stable frequency reference for the circuit. In many digital systems, the crystal is connected to an oscillator circuit inside an MCU, processor, or other IC. A common configuration is the Pierce oscillator, where the crystal works together with two load capacitors to form the oscillation loop. The crystal itself can be considered as a high-Q resonant component. This means that even small changes in the surrounding circuit can affect its behavior. Therefore, crystal oscillator PCB layout is not simply about placing the component close to the IC. The routing, ground plane, surrounding copper, and parasitic effects also need to be considered. （Piezoelectric Effect） 2. Why Should You Avoid Traces Under a Crystal Oscillator? The area around a crystal oscillator may look electrically simple, but PCB routing underneath the crystal can introduce several unwanted effects. Parasitic Capacitance A PCB trace running underneath the crystal or its oscillator pins can form parasitic capacitance with the copper layers below or above it. This additional capacitance changes the effective load seen by the oscillator circuit. As a result, the crystal's oscillation frequency may shift, and the startup characteristics can also be affected. This is especially important because the crystal oscillator circuit usually operates with relatively small signal levels and is sensitive to its load conditions. Keeping unnecessary copper and traces away from the crystal area helps reduce these unpredictable parasitic effects. （recommend pcb layout） Noise Coupling High-speed signal traces can generate rapidly changing electric fields. If these traces pass beneath or too close to the crystal oscillator, noise can couple into the sensitive oscillation loop through parasitic capacitance. The problem becomes more noticeable when the nearby traces carry high-speed clocks, switching signals, or other signals with large voltage transitions. For this reason, good PCB routing practice is to keep noisy signal traces away from the crystal and its oscillator pins. EMI and Signal Integrity The crystal oscillator area should also be treated as a sensitive clock source. Poor routing can increase unwanted coupling between the oscillator and nearby circuits. At the same time, the crystal circuit itself can become a source of electromagnetic radiation if its return path and surrounding copper are not properly controlled. A compact layout with short connections and a clean reference plane can help reduce both noise coupling and EMI risks. （Sources of EMI Issues） 3. Why Use a Guard Ring and Grounding Vias? In addition to keeping signal traces away, some designs use a grounded copper guard ring around the crystal oscillator. Guard Ring A guard ring is a copper area surrounding the sensitive crystal circuit and connected to ground. Its purpose is to provide a low-impedance ground barrier around the oscillator area, helping reduce coupling from nearby signals. The guard ring should not replace the basic keep-out requirements. It is an additional measure for improving isolation and controlling the electromagnetic environment around the crystal. （Ground Guard Ring） Grounding Via Stitching Grounding vias can be placed around the guard ring to connect the surrounding ground copper to the ground planes on other layers. This via stitching helps maintain a more continuous ground structure and can reduce the path through which external noise couples into the oscillator area. However, adding more vias does not automatically make the design better. The via placement should be coordinated with the crystal package, oscillator pins, routing space, and PCB manufacturing requirements. （Ground Stitching Vias） Keep-Out Area The most basic rule is still to keep unnecessary signal traces and copper away from the crystal and its oscillator pins. The exact keep-out size depends on the crystal, IC, PCB stackup, operating frequency, and layout requirements. Therefore, the IC or crystal manufacturer's recommendations should be followed whenever available. A typical layout can be organized as: Crystal → Short oscillator traces → Load capacitors → IC. The surrounding area can then use a grounded guard ring and stitching vias where necessary. （typical crystal pcb layout） 4. Crystal Oscillator PCB Layout and Routing Tips Good crystal oscillator PCB layout focuses on keeping the oscillation loop short, quiet, and predictable. Place the Crystal Close to the IC The crystal should normally be placed as close as practical to the corresponding oscillator pins of the MCU or other IC. Shorter connections reduce parasitic capacitance and inductance and help minimize the area of the sensitive oscillator loop. Avoid placing the crystal far away and routing long traces back to the IC. Keep Oscillator Routing Short and Symmetrical The traces between the crystal and the oscillator pins should be as short as practical. Avoid unnecessary vias, sharp detours, and long parallel runs with noisy signals. When possible, keep the two oscillator connections reasonably symmetrical to reduce differences in parasitic effects. Place Load Capacitors Close to the Oscillator Pins Load capacitors are normally placed close to the crystal and IC oscillator pins. Long traces between the capacitors and the IC add parasitic inductance and capacitance, making the actual load different from the nominal capacitor value. Therefore, component placement and PCB routing should be considered together rather than separately. Avoid High-Speed Traces Near the Crystal During PCB routing, keep high-speed clocks, switching nodes, power converters, and other noisy signals away from the crystal area whenever possible. If a high-speed signal must cross the region, consider whether the routing can be changed to maintain sufficient physical separation. This is particularly important for dense multilayer boards where signals on adjacent layers may also couple through the dielectric. Provide a Clean Ground Reference A continuous ground plane can provide a stable reference for the surrounding circuit and help control return-current paths. However, avoid routing unrelated signals through the sensitive crystal area on other layers. The goal is not simply to create as much copper as possible, but to create a predictable electromagnetic environment around the oscillator. Consider the Crystal Package and Shielding For some applications, the crystal oscillator may be enclosed in a metal package or shielded structure. If shielding is used, make sure its connection to ground is reliable and that the mechanical structure does not introduce unexpected parasitic effects. For designs with strict clock stability or EMI requirements, testing should be used to verify the actual performance rather than relying only on layout rules. 5. Common Mistakes in Crystal Oscillator PCB Routing Several layout mistakes can make an otherwise functional crystal oscillator less stable. Running signal traces directly underneath the crystal. Routing high-speed or switching signals too close to the oscillator loop. Placing the crystal too far from the IC. Using unnecessarily long oscillator traces. Placing load capacitors far from the oscillator pins. Adding excessive vias or complicated routing around the crystal. Ignoring the IC manufacturer's crystal layout recommendations. These problems may not always cause an immediate failure. In some designs, the oscillator may still start normally but show frequency deviation, increased sensitivity to noise, or different behavior between PCB revisions. That is why crystal oscillator layout should be treated as a complete circuit rather than simply a component placement rule. The rule of “no traces under the crystal oscillator” is not an absolute manufacturing requirement. Its purpose is to reduce parasitic capacitance, noise coupling, and interference around a sensitive oscillator circuit. In practical PCB routing , the most important principles are to keep the crystal close to the IC, minimize the oscillator loop, keep noisy signals away, place load capacitors properly, and provide a clean ground environment. For more demanding designs, a grounded guard ring and via stitching can provide additional isolation. Ultimately, the recommended layout from the IC and crystal manufacturers should be used as the primary reference, with actual testing used to verify oscillator stability and EMI performance. Keep Oscillator Routing Short and Symmetrical The traces between the crystal and the oscillator pins should be as short as practical. Avoid unnecessary vias, sharp detours, and long parallel runs with noisy signals. When possible, keep the two oscillator connections reasonably symmetrical to reduce differences in parasitic effects. Place Load Capacitors Close to the Oscillator Pins Load capacitors are normally placed close to the crystal and IC oscillator pins. Long traces between the capacitors and the IC add parasitic inductance and capacitance, making the actual load different from the nominal capacitor value. Therefore, component placement and PCB routing should be considered together rather than separately. Avoid High-Speed Traces Near the Crystal During PCB routing, keep high-speed clocks, switching nodes, power converters, and other noisy signals away from the crystal area whenever possible. If a high-speed signal must cross the region, consider whether the routing can be changed to maintain sufficient physical separation. This is particularly important for dense multilayer boards where signals on adjacent layers may also couple through the dielectric. Provide a Clean Ground Reference A continuous ground plane can provide a stable reference for the surrounding circuit and help control return-current paths. However, avoid routing unrelated signals through the sensitive crystal area on other layers. The goal is not simply to create as much copper as possible, but to create a predictable electromagnetic environment around the oscillator. Consider the Crystal Package and Shielding For some applications, the crystal oscillator may be enclosed in a metal package or shielded structure. If shielding is used, make sure its connection to ground is reliable and that the mechanical structure does not introduce unexpected parasitic effects. For designs with strict clock stability or EMI requirements, testing should be used to verify the actual performance rather than relying only on layout rules. 5. Common Mistakes in Crystal Oscillator PCB Routing Several layout mistakes can make an otherwise functional crystal oscillator less stable. Running signal traces directly underneath the crystal. Routing high-speed or switching signals too close to the oscillator loop. Placing the crystal too far from the IC. Using unnecessarily long oscillator traces. Placing load capacitors far from the oscillator pins. Adding excessive vias or complicated routing around the crystal. Ignoring the IC manufacturer's crystal layout recommendations. These problems may not always cause an immediate failure. In some designs, the oscillator may still start normally but show frequency deviation, increased sensitivity to noise, or different behavior between PCB revisions. That is why crystal oscillator layout should be treated as a complete circuit rather than simply a component placement rule. The rule of “no traces under the crystal oscillator” is not an absolute manufacturing requirement. Its purpose is to reduce parasitic capacitance, noise coupling, and interference around a sensitive oscillator circuit. In practical PCB routing , the most important principles are to keep the crystal close to the IC, minimize the oscillator loop, keep noisy signals away, place load capacitors properly, and provide a clean ground environment. For more demanding designs, a grounded guard ring and via stitching can provide additional isolation. Ultimately, the recommended layout from the IC and crystal manufacturers should be used as the primary reference, with actual testing used to verify oscillator stability and EMI performance. How to Generate Gerber Files in Fusion 360? by: Mia Nov 23,2023 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Design Tutorial Gerber Fusion 360 Autodesk Once you have completed the PCB design in Fusion 360, the next step is to export production files to prepare for PCB manufacturing. Therefore, this tutorial will guide you on how to export Gerber files and Drill files in Autodesk Fusion 360. This guide uses the demo board example in Fusion 360 named "Air_Quality_Sensor." In Fusion 360, there are three options for exporting Gerber files: CAM Preview, CAM Processor, and Export Gerber, NC Drill, Assembly and Drawing Outputs. As shown in the following image: Method One: Click on "CAM Preview" to Initiate the Export • Select "MANUFACTURING" -> "MANUFACTURING" -> "CAM Preview" • The Manufacturing Preview window will appear, then click on the CAM Processor button in the bottom right corner, as shown in the following image. • After the CAM Processor window appears, click on the document icon next to the CAM file name, then choose "Load CAM jobs" -> "examples" and select the CAM file that suits your design. Since it is a 2-layer board, we select "example_2_layer.cam." • On the left side of the window, select "Gerber", and keep the Output Type as the default "Gerber RS-274X". Click on the "Process Job" button in the bottom right corner, and choose the desired pathway for saving. • The generated files are as follows: Method Two: Click on "CAM Processor" to Initiate the Export • Select "MANUFACTURING" -> "MANUFACTURING" -> "CAM Processor" After clicking, the CAM Processor window will appear. The subsequent steps are the same as the steps in Method One. Method Three: Click on "Export Gerber, NC Drill, Assembly and Drawing Outputs" to Initiate the Export • Select "MANUFACTURING" -> "MANUFACTURING" -> "Export Gerber, NC Drill, Assembly and Drawing Outputs" • After clicking, the CAM Export File List window will appear. You can see various files such as profile, copper, soldermask, solderpaste, drill files, and more, which are the Gerber files. • Click OK, select the destination where you want to save the files, then click Save. And then the Gerber files will be exported and saved. • A ZIP folder containing all the necessary PCB Gerber files will be generated. • If you want to check what is inside this ZIP folder, simply right-click on the ZIP folder and extract all the files. At this point, you have completed all the steps on how to generate Gerber and drill files using Autodesk Fusion 360. Generate Gerber, Drill File and Centroid File (PnP File) Open the control panel of Eagle and select "File"->"Open"->"Board". Choose the .brd file you want to use. This guide uses the board example provided by the Eagle. The name of the file is Arduino_MEGA2560_ref.brd. At this point, a window displaying the PCB layout will appear, as shown in the following image: Click on the CAM Processor button on the toolbar (the one without the green arrow), or select "File"->"CAM Processor". Tips: To avoid potential manufacturing issues, it is highly recommended to perform a DRC check before exporting Gerber files. Click on the document icon next to the CAM file name, and then select "Load CAM jobs"->"examples". Choose the CAM file that is suitable for your design. Here, since we are working with a 2-layer board, we select "example_2_layer.cam". Use the Gerber previewer on the right-hand side to inspect the data exported in each layer of the Gerber files. Then, check the "Export as ZIP" option and click "Process Job" to proceed. Note：Please uncheck the box of "Negative image", as indicated by the red box in the following figure. This will generate a ZIP folder containing all the necessary PCB Gerber files. If you want to check what is inside this ZIP folder, then just right-click on the ZIP folder and extract all the files. And that concludes all the steps on how to generate Gerber and drill files using Eagle 9.6.2 version. The centroid file (PnP file) is under the Assembly folder. Generate Gerber, Drill File and Centroid File (PnP File) Open the control panel of Eagle and select "File"->"Open"->"Board". Choose the .brd file you want to use. This guide uses the board example provided by the Eagle. The name of the file is Arduino_MEGA2560_ref.brd. At this point, a window displaying the PCB layout will appear, as shown in the following image: Click on the CAM Processor button on the toolbar (the one without the green arrow), or select "File"->"CAM Processor". Tips: To avoid potential manufacturing issues, it is highly recommended to perform a DRC check before exporting Gerber files. Click on the document icon next to the CAM file name, and then select "Load CAM jobs"->"examples". Choose the CAM file that is suitable for your design. Here, since we are working with a 2-layer board, we select "example_2_layer.cam". Use the Gerber previewer on the right-hand side to inspect the data exported in each layer of the Gerber files. Then, check the "Export as ZIP" option and click "Process Job" to proceed. Note：Please uncheck the box of "Negative image", as indicated by the red box in the following figure. This will generate a ZIP folder containing all the necessary PCB Gerber files. If you want to check what is inside this ZIP folder, then just right-click on the ZIP folder and extract all the files. And that concludes all the steps on how to generate Gerber and drill files using Eagle 9.6.2 version. The centroid file (PnP file) is under the Assembly folder. This article uses the demo project provided with the KiCad software. All steps have been tested in KiCad version 7.0.0, and there may be slight variations if using a different version of KiCad. Generate Gerber Tips: To avoid some potential manufacturing issues, it is strongly recommended to perform a DRC (Design Rule Check) before exporting Gerber files. Open the PCB file with the extension .kicad_pcb, then click on "File" -> "Fabrication Outputs" -> "Gerbers (.gbr)..." as shown in the following image. After clicking, the Gerber setup window will appear as shown in the following image. Please refer to the image below for the settings. Next, click on the "Plot" button at the bottom of the window. All generated Gerber files will be placed in the target folder you specified earlier. If there are expired zone fills and you forgot to refill them, when you have checked the "Check zone fills before plotting" option, KiCad will prompt you for confirmation. Simply click on "Refill", and the file generation process will continue. Generate Drill Files In the Gerber generation window, click on "Generate Drill Files..." located in the bottom right corner. This will open the Drill file settings window, as shown in the image below. Please refer to the image for the settings. Next, click on the "Generate Drill Files" button at the bottom of the window. All generated Drill files will be placed in the target folder you specified earlier. At this point, the export of Gerber files and Drill files is complete. By default, they are usually placed in a folder named "CAM" within the directory where the PCB file is located. The Gerber files can be found within this folder, as shown in the following image. How to Set Shortcut Key in Cadence Allegro PCB Editor? by: Mia Sep 25,2023 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Design Tutorial shortcut key Allegro PCB Editor Setting shortcut key in Allegro can significantly improve work efficiency and lower body burden. In this article, we will introduce the three methods to set shortcut key: Directly defined in the Allegro PCB Editor command window; By modifying the user variable env file; Define strokes as shortcut keys. Directly Defined in the Allegro PCB Editor Command Window This kind of shortcut key can only be used in the present design and will be invalid if restarting the software. The command format is as follows: alias F2 add connect funckey a add connect For example, set the shortcut key for routing command. As shown in the figure below, enter alias F2 add connect in the command window, and press Enter to use it. There are two ways that allow us to check which commands can be set as shortcut keys: 1.Directly enter alias or funckey in the command window, and press Enter to pop up the shortcut key dialog box, as shown below: 2.View it by executing the Tools->Utilities->Keyboard Commands command, as shown below: By Modifying the User Variable env File There are two modes for this: alias and funckey. If you use alias to define letters, you will need to enter the letter and press Enter for the shortcut to take effect. It is recommended not to define letters and instead use something like Fn or Del for quicker access. The funckey command can be used to define individual shortcut key, and it is more powerful than alias. Anything that can be defined with alias can also be defined with funckey. Funckey definitions are case-sensitive. For example, funckey C 'dbdoctor' assigns dbdoctor to the uppercase C, while funckey c 'copy' assigns copy to the lowercase c. Funckey can also define two letters. For example, when we move the device and align the structure, select the center of the positioning hole, and set it as follows: funckey sa "prepopup;pop dyn_option_select 'Snap pick to@:@Arc/Circle Center'", which is quite convenient. env File Path Taking my computer as an example, in D:\Cadence\SPB_Data\pcbenv, open the env file with Notepad and you can add your own shortcut. Note: Please back up the env file before modifying it. Open the env file with Notepad, as shown in the picture below. In the red box are several of my customized shortcut keys. Users can define shortcut keys according to their own operating habits. Define Strokes as Shortcut Keys Create allegro stroke. Execute Tools->Utilities->Stroke Editor command. After that, a window like the one below will pop up. You can use the right mouse button to draw the strokes you want to define in the blank area of the window and enter the content for the command, as shown in the figure below. In my case, I drew a line with the right mouse button and set the command as oops. After setting it up, if we want to perform the oops operation in the future, we can simply draw a line with the right mouse button. Make sure the stroke is activated. Setup->User Preferences Editor>UI>input Check the no_dragpopup option, otherwise, you need to hold down the Ctrl key to take effect. Enter the year of your birth and check your Chinese Zodiac.
